title: Mesopotamia and Egypt
bigQuestion: How did two rivers and one great river turn farming villages into the first cities, kingdoms and written laws?

story.title: The First Day in the Tablet House
story.kicker: About four thousand years ago, a boy in a Sumerian city walked to school with a lump of wet clay and a very sore future.
paragraphs: The boy wakes before dawn in a mud-brick house in the city of Nippur, in the land between the rivers. His mother hands him two rolls of bread and a jar of water. His father is a scribe, a man who writes for a living, and today the boy begins learning the trade. He walks through narrow streets already loud with donkeys and merchants to a house the Sumerians called the edubba, the tablet house.

Inside, boys sit on benches of packed earth. Each holds a smooth lump of damp clay, patted into a tablet the size of a hand. The teacher, called the father of the tablet house, writes a line of signs on one side with a reed cut to a wedge-shaped tip. The boy must copy it on the other side. Each sign is a bundle of small wedges pressed into the clay. There are hundreds of signs, and he will spend years learning them.

The first lessons are lists: names of trees, then stones, then animals, then gods. Later come words for grain measures and the bad-tempered letters of merchants. Because the language of learning, Sumerian, is already old-fashioned, many boys speak Akkadian at home and must learn Sumerian as a second tongue. Mistakes are corrected with a cane. One surviving text has a student complaining that he was beaten for talking, for standing up, for bad handwriting and for walking through the gate wrong.

At day's end the boy's tablet is scraped smooth and set aside to be used again. But some tablets were baked, by accident when a house burned or on purpose to make a record last. Those survived under the sand for four thousand years. When archaeologists dug them up, they found the lists, the exercises and the complaint about the cane. The boy's sore fingers are the reason we can read his world.
story.think: The student's complaint about school is one of the oldest personal writings we have. Why might a record of an ordinary bad day tell historians more than a king's monument?

lessons.title: Two Rivers and One Great River
lessons.mainIdea: The first civilizations grew in the valleys of the Tigris, Euphrates and Nile, where rivers gave water, rich soil and a road for boats.
reading: Look at a map of the Middle East and northeast Africa. Most of it is desert. But three rivers cut through the dry land, and along them the first cities in the world appeared. The *Tigris* and the *Euphrates* flow from the mountains of Turkey southeast to the Persian Gulf. The land between them the Greeks later called *Mesopotamia*, which means between the rivers. Today most of it is Iraq. Far to the west, the *Nile* flows north out of Africa through Egypt to the Mediterranean Sea.

A river in a desert is life. It gives drinking water for people and animals. It gives water for crops, in a place where rain alone would grow nothing. When it floods it spreads a layer of fine mud called silt over the fields, and silt is rich soil. The Nile is the longest river in the world at roughly four thousand miles, and it flooded every summer so regularly that Egyptians set their calendar by it. The Greek historian Herodotus wrote that Egypt was a gift of the river.

A river is also a road. Grain, timber, stone and copper are heavy. Carrying them on a donkey's back is slow, but a boat can float tons of cargo downstream with little effort. On the Nile the current runs north while the wind usually blows south, so boats could sail up and drift down. Cities on rivers could gather food and goods from hundreds of miles away.

Mesopotamia and Egypt were alike in depending on rivers, but the rivers were not alike. The Nile's flood came on time and gently. The Tigris and Euphrates flooded in spring, often violently, sometimes too early or too late for the crops. Egypt was protected by deserts on both sides. Mesopotamia was open plain, easy to invade. Those differences shaped how each civilization thought about its gods, its kings and its future.

words.d: the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, mostly in modern Iraq
fine, rich mud left on fields by a flooding river
the river that flows north through Egypt to the Mediterranean, the longest river in the world

look.title: Three Rivers of the Ancient World
look.prompt: Length alone does not make a river useful. What else about the Nile made it a better foundation for a civilization than a river of the same length in a rainy forest?

check.q: What does the name Mesopotamia mean?
choices: Between the rivers
Land of the pharaohs
Gift of the Nile
The fertile crescent
check.why: Greeks named the land between the Tigris and Euphrates Mesopotamia, which means between the rivers.

check.q: Why was flooding good for farmers along these rivers?
choices: Floods washed away weeds
Floods left behind a layer of rich silt
Floods scared off invaders
Floods filled wells with rainwater
check.why: River floods spread silt, fine mud that is rich soil, across the fields every year.

check.q: How did the Nile and the Mesopotamian rivers differ?
choices: The Nile was shorter than the Tigris
The Nile did not flood at all
The Nile flooded gently and on time; the Tigris and Euphrates flooded violently and unpredictably

check.why: Egypt's flood was regular enough to set a calendar by. Mesopotamia's spring floods came at uncertain times and could destroy fields.

lessons.title: Irrigation and Its Price
lessons.mainIdea: Irrigation let river-valley farmers grow huge harvests, but it required organized labor, shared rules and constant repair.
reading: Rivers do not water fields by themselves. Farmers had to dig canals to carry water from the river to the land, and ditches to spread it between the crops. They built earth banks to hold back floods, and gates to open and close the flow. This system is called *irrigation*. In southern Mesopotamia almost no rain falls, so every field of barley depended on a canal someone had dug and someone kept clean.

Canals silt up. Banks wash out. A gate left open drowns one field and starves another. Irrigation therefore needed cooperation on a scale a village had never seen. Hundreds of people had to dig at the same time, follow a plan, and agree on who got water first. Someone had to organize the work and settle the fights. Historians argue that this need for organization helped create the first governments. A king who controlled the water controlled the food.

In Egypt, the Nile did much of the work. Farmers built low banks to divide the floodplain into basins. When the flood came, they let water into the basins, held it there for weeks so the silt could settle, then let it drain. This is called basin irrigation. It needed less digging than Mesopotamia's canals, but still needed officials to measure the flood, record the fields and collect a share of the harvest as *tax*.

Irrigation had a hidden cost. River water carries tiny amounts of salt. When water evaporates from a field, the salt stays behind. Over centuries, fields in southern Mesopotamia grew salty, and farmers switched from wheat, which hates salt, to barley, which tolerates it. Records show harvests falling. Some of the oldest cities were slowly starved by the very system that had fed them.

words.d: bringing water to fields through canals, ditches and gates
a channel dug to carry water from a river to fields or to boats
a share of harvest, goods or money that people must give to their rulers

look.title: The Canal Meeting
look.text: Three villages share one canal. The upstream village takes water first and plants extra fields. By the time water reaches the downstream village, the flow is a trickle. The middle village says the canal bank near the upstream village is leaking and nobody has fixed it.
look.prompt: What rules would the three villages need to agree on? Who could enforce them? How might this situation lead to a king?

check.q: Why did irrigation push people toward organized government?
choices: Canals could be dug by one family alone
Irrigation required no planning
Gods ordered people to build canals
Canals needed large groups working to a plan and rules about sharing water
check.why: Digging, repairing and sharing a canal system needed cooperation and someone with authority to organize it.

check.q: How did Egyptian basin irrigation work?
choices: Flood water was held in banked fields until silt settled, then drained
Water was pumped uphill by machines
Farmers carried water in jars from the Nile
Rain was collected in stone tanks
check.why: Egyptians divided the floodplain with low banks, trapped the flood there, and let it drain after the silt settled.

check.q: What long-term problem did irrigation cause in southern Mesopotamia?
choices: The rivers dried up completely
Salt built up in the soil and harvests fell
Canals grew too large to cross
Fields became too wet to plant
check.why: Evaporating river water left salt behind. Over centuries fields grew salty and crops shrank.

lessons.title: Sumer's City-States
lessons.mainIdea: By about 3000 BCE, Sumer in southern Mesopotamia had a dozen independent walled cities, each ruled by its own king and its own god.
reading: The first cities on Earth rose in *Sumer*, the southern end of Mesopotamia near the Persian Gulf. By around 3200 BCE the city of Uruk had walls, temples and a population in the tens of thousands, larger than any place people had ever lived. Others followed: Ur, Lagash, Kish, Nippur, Eridu. Each was a *city-state*, meaning a city that ruled itself and the farmland around it, like a tiny country. There was no united Sumerian nation, only rival cities that traded, quarreled and fought.

Each city belonged to a god. Ur was the city of the moon god Nanna; Uruk belonged to the sky god An and the goddess Inanna. The god's temple stood on a raised platform in the center, and its priests owned large farms and workshops. Much of the city's grain flowed into temple storehouses and out again as rations to workers. A king, called a lugal, meaning big man, led the army and claimed to rule on the god's behalf.

Inside the walls, life was crowded and unequal. At the top were the king, priests and nobles. Below them were free farmers, merchants, craftsmen and scribes. At the bottom were enslaved people, mostly prisoners of war or people sold for debt. Women could own property and run businesses, and a few priestesses held great power, but men held nearly all political offices.

The city-states fought over water and land for centuries. Around 2334 BCE, a ruler named Sargon from the city of Akkad conquered all of them. He built the first *empire*, a state ruling many peoples. His daughter Enheduanna was a high priestess who wrote hymns. She is the first author in history whose name we know. Sargon's empire lasted about a century and a half, then broke apart. But the idea of one ruler over many cities never went away.

words.d: the region of southern Mesopotamia where the first cities were built
a city that governs itself and the land around it, like a small country
a state that rules many different peoples and lands under one ruler

look.title: Inside the Walls of Ur
look.text: Imagine climbing Ur's wall around 2500 BCE. Inside, mud-brick houses press against one another along twisting lanes. In the center a temple rises on a platform. Outside, canals fan out through barley fields, and beyond them lies a rival city's land.
look.prompt: Why would a city need a wall? Why might two cities twenty miles apart end up at war rather than joining together?

check.q: What is a city-state?
choices: A capital city of a large nation
A city with no government
A city that rules itself and the farmland around it
A state made of many cities under one king
check.why: Each Sumerian city was independent, with its own king, god and surrounding fields, like a tiny country.

check.q: Who is Enheduanna?
choices: The moon goddess of Ur
A queen who ruled Uruk
The scribe who invented cuneiform
A priestess and the first known author in history
check.why: Enheduanna, daughter of Sargon of Akkad, wrote hymns and is the earliest author whose name survives.

check.q: What did Sargon of Akkad do around 2334 BCE?
choices: Conquered the Sumerian city-states and built the first empire
Built the first ziggurat
Wrote the first law code
Founded the city of Uruk
check.why: Sargon united the rival cities under one rule, creating the first state that governed many peoples.

lessons.title: Cuneiform: Writing on Clay
lessons.mainIdea: Sumerians invented writing around 3200 BCE to keep records, and their wedge-shaped script was used for three thousand years.
reading: Writing was not invented to tell stories. It was invented to count. Temple officials in Uruk needed to track how many jars of oil came in, how many sheep went out and who owed what. At first they pressed small clay tokens into shapes and scratched pictures on clay to stand for goods. By about 3200 BCE, those pictures had become a system: a sign for sheep, a sign for the number ten, a sign for the temple. The oldest writing in the world is mostly receipts.

Over centuries the pictures turned into wedges. A scribe pressed the corner of a cut reed into wet clay, making short straight marks. Because the marks look like wedges, we call the script *cuneiform*, from a Latin word for wedge. The signs stopped looking like objects and began to stand for sounds and syllables. That made it possible to write any word, including names, poems and laws. A fully trained scribe knew several hundred signs.

Cuneiform outlived Sumer. Akkadians, Babylonians, Assyrians, Hittites and Persians all adapted it for their own languages. It was used for about three thousand years, longer than the alphabet has existed so far. Hundreds of thousands of tablets survive: school exercises, contracts, letters, medical texts, star observations and the Epic of Gilgamesh, a long poem about a king of Uruk who searches for a way to escape death.

For two thousand years nobody could read it. In the 1800s, a British officer named Henry Rawlinson copied a huge inscription carved on a cliff at Behistun in Iran. It was written in three languages. Using the Persian version as a key, he and others cracked the Babylonian cuneiform. In 1872, a museum worker named George Smith read a tablet describing a great flood and a boat full of animals. It was older than the Bible. The story goes that he was so excited he began to undress in the reading room.

words.d: the wedge-shaped writing of Mesopotamia, pressed into clay with a reed
a person trained to read and write, who kept records for temples, kings and merchants
one beat of a spoken word, such as the two beats in wa-ter

look.title: A Student's Bad Day
look.text: A Sumerian school text tells of a student who describes his day: he recited his tablet, ate his lunch, made a new tablet and wrote it. Then he lists his beatings: the man in charge of the gate beat him, the man in charge of the courtyard beat him, and his teacher beat him for poor handwriting.
look.cite: Sumerian school text known as Schooldays, about 2000 BCE (paraphrased from modern translations)
look.prompt: This text was copied by students as a writing exercise. Why might teachers have wanted students to copy a story about being beaten at school?

check.q: What was writing first used for in Sumer?
choices: Telling myths about the gods
Keeping records of goods, animals and debts
Writing letters between kings
Carving names on tombs
check.why: The earliest tablets are accounts: counts of sheep, grain and oil for the temples of Uruk.

check.q: Why is the script called cuneiform?
choices: It was invented in a city called Cunei
It was written on cones of clay
Its marks are wedge-shaped
It could only be read by priests
check.why: Cuneiform comes from a Latin word for wedge, because a reed pressed into clay leaves wedge-shaped marks.

check.q: How did scholars finally learn to read cuneiform?
choices: They found a dictionary in a Sumerian library
They asked people in Iraq who still used it
They guessed from the pictures
They used a cliff inscription written in three languages as a key
check.why: The Behistun inscription repeated the same text in Persian and Babylonian, and the known Persian version unlocked the rest.

lessons.title: Wheels, Bronze and Ziggurats
lessons.mainIdea: Sumerians used the wheel, bronze tools and monumental temples called ziggurats, inventions that spread far beyond Mesopotamia.
reading: The wheel seems obvious, but people farmed for thousands of years without it. The first wheels were potter's wheels, turntables for shaping clay, in use in Mesopotamia by about 3500 BCE. Soon after, someone set two solid wooden disks on an axle under a cart. Wheeled carts and war chariots pulled by donkeys appear in Sumerian art by about 2500 BCE. A cart lets one animal haul what ten people could carry. The idea spread across Europe and Asia, though not to the Americas, which had no animals to pull one.

Sumerians also learned to mix copper with a little tin to make *bronze*, a metal harder than either. Bronze tools held an edge that stone could not. Bronze swords, helmets and axes changed war. But tin was rare and came from far away, so bronze was expensive, and the age named for it, the Bronze Age, was also an age of long-distance trade. A city that lost its trade routes lost its weapons.

The most visible Sumerian invention was the *ziggurat*. It was a temple built on a stepped platform of mud brick, rising in terraces like a stair-stepped mountain. The god's shrine sat on top. King Ur-Nammu built the great ziggurat of Ur around 2100 BCE. After four thousand years it still stands more than sixty feet high. Its base is about the size of a football field. In a flat land, the ziggurat was the only mountain. It told everyone who walked by which city was strongest.

Other Sumerian tools were quieter. They divided the hour into sixty minutes and the circle into three hundred sixty degrees, and we still do. They kept records of the planets. They used a plow pulled by oxen and a seed drill that dropped grain into the furrow. Each invention fed the next: the plow made surplus, surplus paid for bronze, bronze built armies, armies needed scribes to count them.

words.d: a hard metal made by mixing copper with a little tin
a Mesopotamian temple built on a stepped platform of mud brick
the rod that a wheel turns on

look.title: Sixty Seconds
look.text: Look at a clock. Sixty seconds make a minute, sixty minutes make an hour. A circle has three hundred sixty degrees. These numbers come from Sumerian counting, which used sixty as a base because it divides evenly by two, three, four, five, six, ten, twelve, fifteen, twenty and thirty.
look.prompt: Why would a base of sixty be handy for people dividing up grain, land and hours? Why do you think we never switched to a base of ten for time?

check.q: What were the first wheels used for?
choices: Shaping pottery on a turntable
Chariots in war
Grinding grain
Lifting water from canals
check.why: Potter's wheels came first, around 3500 BCE. Carts with wheels appeared later.

check.q: Why was bronze expensive?
choices: It had to be imported already made from Egypt
Tin was rare and came from far away
Copper could not be found in Mesopotamia
Only kings were allowed to own it
check.why: Bronze needs tin, which Mesopotamia lacked. Trading for tin over long distances made bronze costly.

check.q: What was a ziggurat?
choices: A king's tomb
A city wall
A stepped temple platform with a shrine on top
A canal gate
check.why: A ziggurat was a mud-brick temple built in terraces like a stair-stepped mountain, with the god's shrine at the top.

lessons.title: Hammurabi's Code
lessons.mainIdea: Around 1750 BCE, King Hammurabi of Babylon had nearly three hundred laws carved in stone, showing that justice depended on your rank.
reading: Hammurabi was king of Babylon, a city on the Euphrates, from about 1792 to 1750 BCE. He conquered most of Mesopotamia. Near the end of his reign he had a set of laws carved on a black stone pillar over seven feet tall. He set it up where people could see it. At the top, a carving shows the sun god Shamash, god of justice. He is handing Hammurabi the tools of a ruler. The message was clear: these laws come from the gods, and the king enforces them.

The *code* contains about two hundred eighty-two laws. They cover almost everything: wages, rents, theft, marriage, divorce, adoption, medical fees, the duties of builders and boatmen, and what happens when an ox gores someone. Many laws follow the pattern if this happens, then that must be done. Some protect the weak: a widow keeps her home, and a debtor's family cannot be held as slaves forever. Others are brutal, with death as the penalty for many crimes.

The most famous laws are the ones about injury. If a man puts out the eye of another man, his own eye is put out. If he breaks a bone, his bone is broken. This idea, an eye for an eye, is called retaliation. But it applied only between equals. If a noble injured a commoner, he paid a fine in silver. If he injured an enslaved person, he paid the owner. The same act had three different prices, depending on who was hurt. Justice was real, but it was not equal.

French archaeologists found the stone in 1901 in Susa, Iran. A later conqueror had carried it off there as loot. It now stands in the Louvre museum in Paris. It is not the oldest law code, but it is the most complete. It tells us what a Mesopotamian king thought a ruler owed his people. He owed them order, protection, and a public list of rules that applied even to the powerful.

words.d: an organized set of written laws
paying back an injury with the same injury
a city on the Euphrates that became the capital of Hammurabi's kingdom

look.title: Law 196
look.text: If a man put out the eye of another man, his eye shall be put out.
look.cite: Code of Hammurabi, law 196, about 1750 BCE, translated by L. W. King, 1915
look.prompt: The next laws give a fine in silver if the victim was a commoner and a smaller payment if the victim was enslaved. What does that tell you about how Babylonians thought about people?

check.q: Why was the carving of the sun god placed at the top of Hammurabi's pillar?
choices: To show the laws were a gift from Egypt
To warn people that the sun could blind them
To decorate the stone for the museum
To show the laws had the authority of the gods
check.why: The image of Shamash handing Hammurabi a rod and ring told viewers that the king ruled and judged on the gods' behalf.

check.q: Which statement best describes justice under the code?
choices: The punishment depended on the rank of the victim
Everyone received exactly the same punishment
Only enslaved people were punished
Only nobles could be punished
check.why: The same injury cost an eye, a fine, or a smaller payment depending on whether the victim was a noble, a commoner or enslaved.

check.q: Where was the stone found, and why was it there?
choices: In Babylon, where it had always stood
In Susa, Iran, carried off by a later conqueror
In Egypt, sent as a gift
In Paris, where it was carved
check.why: A later king looted the pillar and took it to Susa. French archaeologists found it there in 1901.

lessons.title: Three Kingdoms on the Nile
lessons.mainIdea: Egypt was united around 3100 BCE and its long history is divided into the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms, separated by times of breakdown.
reading: Egypt is a long green ribbon in a brown desert. The Nile valley is often only a few miles wide, and almost everyone lived within sight of the river. Around 3100 BCE a ruler from the south, remembered as Narmer or Menes, united the valley, called Upper Egypt, with the wide delta near the sea, called Lower Egypt. From then on Egypt's ruler wore a double crown, one for each land. That ruler was the *pharaoh*, a word that means great house.

Historians divide Egypt's next two thousand years into three great periods. The *Old Kingdom*, roughly 2686 to 2181 BCE, was the age of the pyramids, when pharaohs had the power and wealth to build the largest stone structures on Earth. It ended in drought, famine and civil war. The Middle Kingdom, roughly 2055 to 1650 BCE, reunited the land. Pharaohs built forts, dug canals and expanded trade. It ended when foreign rulers called the Hyksos, who had horses and chariots, took over the delta.

The *New Kingdom*, roughly 1550 to 1070 BCE, was Egypt's age of empire. Pharaohs drove out the Hyksos, adopted their chariots and pushed armies into Syria and Nubia. This period had the rulers whose names people still know. Hatshepsut, a woman, ruled as pharaoh for about twenty years and sent trading ships south to a land called Punt. Thutmose III fought seventeen campaigns. Akhenaten tried to replace Egypt's many gods with one, the sun disk, and failed. His son Tutankhamun's tomb was found nearly untouched in 1922.

Ramses II ruled for sixty-six years, built temples everywhere and fought the Hittites at Kadesh, then signed with them the oldest surviving peace treaty. After him Egypt slowly weakened. It was ruled by Libyans, Nubians, Assyrians, Persians and finally Greeks and Romans. But for most of three thousand years, the pharaoh, the Nile and the gods held Egypt together with a stability no other ancient state matched.

words.d: the ruler of ancient Egypt, seen as both king and god
the age of the pyramids, roughly 2686 to 2181 BCE
Egypt's age of empire, roughly 1550 to 1070 BCE
the flat, fan-shaped land where a river splits into branches before reaching the sea

look.title: A Ribbon of Green

look.prompt: How might living on a narrow strip with deserts on both sides help one ruler control all of Egypt? How might it also make Egypt hard to attack?

The sun and the moon

The king and the high priest

choices: The New Kingdom
The Middle Kingdom
The Old Kingdom
The Hyksos period

choices: Egypt built its first pyramids

lessons.title: Pyramids and the Afterlife
lessons.mainIdea: Egyptians built pyramids as tombs because they believed the pharaoh's survival after death protected the whole land.
reading: The Great Pyramid at Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE. It was originally about four hundred eighty feet tall, and for nearly four thousand years it was the tallest building on Earth. It contains roughly two million blocks of limestone, many weighing more than a car. Workers cut them with copper tools, dragged them on sleds over wetted sand, and raised them with ramps. The sides face north, south, east and west almost exactly.

Why build such a thing? Egyptians believed that a person's spirit lived on after death, but only if the body was preserved and supplied with what it needed. They dried bodies with salt, wrapped them in linen and placed them in tombs with food, furniture and small figures of servants. This process is *mummification*. The pharaoh was not an ordinary person. He was believed to be a living god, and his safe passage to the afterlife kept the Nile flooding and the land in order.

The pyramids were not built by enslaved people. Archaeologists have dug up the workers' town beside Giza: bakeries, breweries, barracks and a cemetery of laborers buried with honor. Most were farmers who came during the flood season, when the fields were underwater and no farming could be done. They were fed bread, beer, onions and beef, and worked in named gangs. One team called itself the Friends of Khufu. Building the tomb was a kind of tax, paid in labor.

By the New Kingdom, pharaohs stopped building pyramids, which were easy to find and rob. They cut their tombs into cliffs in the Valley of the Kings near Thebes. Nearly all were looted in ancient times. In 1922 the British archaeologist Howard Carter opened the tomb of the young pharaoh Tutankhamun. It was almost the only one still full. Inside were a golden mask, chariots, beds, games and food for a journey that never ended.

words.d: a massive stone tomb with four sloping sides, built for Old Kingdom pharaohs
drying and wrapping a body so it will not decay
life after death, which Egyptians believed continued if the body was preserved

look.title: The Great Pyramid in Numbers
rows: Years as tallest building on Earth (roughly)
look.prompt: If the pyramid took about twenty years to build, roughly how many blocks had to be set each day? What does that tell you about how the work must have been organized?

check.q: Why did Egyptians preserve bodies as mummies?
choices: They believed the spirit needed the body to live on after death
It stopped diseases from spreading
The desert made burial impossible
Kings wanted to be displayed in museums
check.why: Egyptians believed a person survived death only if the body was preserved and supplied with what it needed.

check.q: Who actually built the pyramids at Giza?
choices: Enslaved captives from Nubia
Farmers working during the flood season, fed and housed in a workers' town
Priests of the sun god
Greek engineers hired by the pharaoh
check.why: The excavated workers' town shows paid, fed laborers, many of them farmers who worked while the fields were flooded.

check.q: Why did New Kingdom pharaohs stop building pyramids?
choices: They ran out of stone
The Nile changed course
Pyramids were easy to find and rob, so they hid their tombs in cliffs
The gods forbade it
check.why: Pyramids advertised the treasure inside. Tombs cut into the Valley of the Kings were meant to be hidden.

lessons.title: Hieroglyphs and the Rosetta Stone
lessons.mainIdea: Egyptian hieroglyphs were unreadable for over a thousand years until a stone with the same text in three scripts let scholars crack them.
reading: Egyptians developed their own writing at about the same time as Sumer. Their formal script is called *hieroglyphs*, from Greek words meaning sacred carving. It uses hundreds of small pictures: an owl, a reed, a pair of legs, a loaf of bread. Some signs stand for whole words. Most stand for sounds. Egyptians carved hieroglyphs on temples and tombs, and wrote a faster, flowing version with reed pens and ink on *papyrus*, a paper made from pressed strips of a river plant.

After Egypt fell under Greek and then Roman rule, fewer and fewer people learned the old script. The last known hieroglyphic inscription was carved in the year 394 CE. After that, for fourteen centuries, no one on Earth could read a single Egyptian sentence. Scholars guessed the pictures were mystical symbols with secret meanings. They were wrong.

In 1799, French soldiers rebuilding a fort near the town of Rashid, which Europeans called Rosetta, dug up a broken slab of dark stone. It was covered with the same announcement, a decree honoring the boy king Ptolemy V in 196 BCE, written three ways: in hieroglyphs, in a later Egyptian script, and in Greek. Greek could be read. The *Rosetta Stone* was the key. When the British defeated the French, they took the stone, and it has been in the British Museum since 1802.

Cracking the code still took more than twenty years. The English scientist Thomas Young showed that some signs spelled out the sound of the name Ptolemy. Then the French scholar Jean-François Champollion, who had learned Coptic, a late form of Egyptian, proved in 1822 that hieroglyphs mixed sound signs and word signs. Suddenly tomb walls, temple pillars and papyrus letters could speak. Three thousand years of Egyptian voices came back.

words.d: the picture-based writing of ancient Egypt
a paper-like material made from pressed strips of a Nile river plant
a slab with the same text in hieroglyphs, a later Egyptian script and Greek, used to decode Egyptian writing

look.title: Three Copies of One Message
look.text: Suppose you find a sign written in a script you cannot read, a second script you cannot read, and English. The English mentions a king's name four times. In the unknown scripts, one group of symbols also appears four times, each time inside an oval.
look.prompt: What would you try first? Why was the name of a king, rather than an ordinary word, the best place to start?

check.q: What does the word hieroglyphs mean?
choices: Wedge writing
River writing
Secret pictures
Sacred carving
check.why: The word comes from Greek for sacred carving, because the script was carved on temples and tombs.

check.q: Why was the Rosetta Stone the key to reading Egyptian?
choices: It carried the same text in Greek, which scholars could read
It was the oldest Egyptian inscription
It contained a dictionary of every sign
It was written by Champollion
check.why: The same decree appeared in three scripts. The Greek version let scholars match sounds and words to the Egyptian signs.

check.q: What did Champollion prove in 1822?
choices: That hieroglyphs were only mystical symbols
That hieroglyphs mixed signs for sounds with signs for words
That Egyptians could not write
That the Rosetta Stone was a fake
check.why: Champollion showed that the script combined sound signs and word signs, which made it possible to read.

sections.title: Living, Trading and Leaving a Legacy

lessons.title: Daily Life: Workers, Women and Scribes
lessons.mainIdea: Most Egyptians and Mesopotamians were farmers, but women, craft workers and scribes each had a distinct place, and we know about them from their own records.
reading: Most people in both lands were farmers who never saw a palace. They lived in mud-brick houses, ate bread, onions, beans, fish and beer, and worked the fields from the end of the flood to the harvest. Children helped from an early age. Few people lived past forty. Sickness was treated with a mix of practical medicine, herbs and prayers to the gods.

Women in Egypt had more legal rights than in most ancient societies. They could own land, run a business, sign contracts, go to court and divorce. Some worked as weavers, brewers, musicians or priestesses. Royal women could hold great power; Hatshepsut ruled as pharaoh. In Mesopotamia, women's rights were narrower and shrank over time, but they too could own property and trade, and some ran taverns or served as priestesses. In both lands, the household was expected to be led by a man.

Scribes stood between the farmers and the king. They recorded taxes, measured fields, wrote letters and kept accounts for temples. A scribe did not have to dig canals or carry bricks. An Egyptian text known as the Satire of the Trades tells a boy to become a scribe by listing the miseries of every other job: the metalworker's burned fingers, the barber's endless walking, the fisherman's fear of crocodiles. Then it says the scribe is the one who gives the orders.

We even know about a strike. At Deir el-Medina, the village of the workers who cut the royal tombs, the grain rations stopped arriving in about 1157 BCE under Ramses III. The workers laid down their tools, marched to a temple and refused to go back until they were paid. A scribe wrote it all down. It is the oldest recorded strike in history, and it worked, at least for a while.

words.d: a fixed amount of food or goods given as pay
when workers stop working together to demand better treatment
a written agreement that a court can enforce

look.title: Why Become a Scribe
look.text: The Satire of the Trades tells a boy to set his heart on writing. It says the potter is caked in mud like a pig, the weaver sits with knees pressed to his chest and cannot breathe, the courier writes his will before leaving because of wild beasts and enemies. But there is no job, it says, without a boss, except the scribe: he is the boss.
look.cite: Egyptian text known as the Satire of the Trades, Middle Kingdom, about 1900 BCE (paraphrased)
look.prompt: This text was written by a scribe and copied by student scribes. How does knowing who wrote it change how much you trust its picture of other jobs?

check.q: Which right did women in ancient Egypt have?
choices: Voting in an assembly
Commanding the army
Owning land and going to court
Serving as scribes in the palace
check.why: Egyptian women could own property, sign contracts, run businesses, go to court and divorce.

check.q: Why did the Satire of the Trades list the miseries of other jobs?
choices: To warn scribes about dangerous work
To record how wages were paid
To argue for better pay for potters
To persuade a boy that being a scribe was the best trade
check.why: The text was a scribe's advertisement for the profession, copied by students learning to write.

check.q: What happened at Deir el-Medina in about 1157 BCE?
choices: Tomb workers stopped work until their overdue rations were paid
The village was destroyed by the Hittites
Hatshepsut was crowned pharaoh
The Rosetta Stone was carved
check.why: When grain rations stopped, the royal tomb workers walked out. A scribe recorded the first known strike.

lessons.title: Trade and War Between Lands
lessons.mainIdea: River civilizations needed goods they lacked, so they traded across great distances and fought over the routes and the wealth.
reading: Mesopotamia had mud, reeds, barley and wool, and almost nothing else. There was no timber, no stone and no metal. So Sumerian merchants sent wool cloth and grain down the Gulf and up the rivers. They brought back cedar from Lebanon, copper from Oman and tin from far to the east. They also brought *lapis lazuli*, a deep blue stone, from the mountains of Afghanistan, more than a thousand miles away. Seals from the Indus cities have been found in Mesopotamian sites, proof of contact between the world's first civilizations.

Egypt was richer in stone and gold but sent ships too. Expeditions went south to *Nubia* for gold, ivory and ebony. Others sailed to a land called Punt for incense and exotic animals. Punt was probably on the coast of the Red Sea or the Horn of Africa. Hatshepsut had her Punt voyage carved on her temple walls. The carvings show the ships, the goods and the people she traded with. Egypt bought cedar from the port of Byblos in Lebanon for ships and coffins.

Trade and war went together. Egypt's New Kingdom armies pushed into Syria partly to control the trade routes there. Around 1274 BCE, Ramses II met the Hittite army at Kadesh in one of the largest chariot battles of the ancient world. Both sides claimed victory. About fifteen years later they signed a treaty, promising peace and to return each other's runaways. A copy in Hittite and a copy in Egyptian both survive.

Mesopotamia's open plain made it a land of conquerors. Akkadians, Amorites, Hittites, Kassites, Assyrians, Babylonians and Persians took turns ruling it. The Assyrians, around 900 to 600 BCE, built the most feared army yet. They had iron weapons and siege engines, and they moved whole conquered peoples to new lands. Their capital at Nineveh held a library of thousands of tablets. It included the best copy of Gilgamesh, saved by being baked when the city burned.

words.d: a deep blue stone from Afghanistan, prized in Mesopotamia and Egypt
a formal written agreement between states
the land south of Egypt along the Nile, rich in gold

look.title: A Merchant's Ledger
look.text: A merchant in Ur about 2000 BCE loads a boat with woolen cloth and silver. Months later he returns with copper ingots. His tablets list every bale and every debt, and one records a complaint that the copper he received was poor quality and that he was treated with contempt.
look.prompt: What does a complaint about bad copper tell you about how far trade had developed? What did the merchant risk on each trip?

check.q: Why did Mesopotamia depend so heavily on trade?
choices: Its people preferred foreign goods
It lacked timber, stone and metal
Its rivers could not be farmed
Its kings forbade farming
check.why: The southern plain had mud, reeds, barley and wool but no wood, stone or metal, all of which had to be imported.

check.q: What does the treaty between Ramses II and the Hittites show?
choices: That Egypt conquered the Hittites
That the Hittites ruled Egypt
That two great powers could end a war with a written agreement
That Egypt had no army
check.why: After a battle both sides claimed to win, the two states signed the oldest surviving peace treaty.

check.q: How did the Nineveh library tablets survive?
choices: They were hidden in a pyramid
They were copied on papyrus
They were sent to Babylon for safekeeping
The fire that destroyed the city baked the clay hard
check.why: When Nineveh burned, the heat baked the clay tablets, which preserved them under the ruins.

lessons.title: What They Left Us
lessons.mainIdea: Writing, written law, the calendar, timekeeping and the idea of the state all came from Mesopotamia and Egypt and are still part of daily life.
reading: Look at the top of a worksheet. There is a date, and the date comes from Egypt. Egyptian priests noticed that the bright star Sirius rose just before the sun at about the time the Nile flood began, once every three hundred sixty-five days. They made a *calendar* of twelve months of thirty days plus five extra days at the end. Julius Caesar borrowed it for Rome, adding a leap day. With small fixes, it is the calendar on your phone.

Now look at a clock. The sixty minutes in each hour come from the Sumerians' counting system based on sixty. The twenty-four hour day comes from Egypt, which divided day and night into twelve parts each. Then look at the words on the page. Alphabets came later, from peoples who traded with Egypt, but the idea that marks can stand for sounds began with cuneiform and hieroglyphs. Every letter you write is a descendant.

The deeper legacy is harder to see. Mesopotamia and Egypt invented the *state*: a government with officials, taxes, records, written law and an army, ruling a large territory. They invented the idea that laws should be written where all can see them, and that a ruler is responsible for justice. They invented the school, the contract, the receipt and the map. They also invented the imperial army, the enslaved war captive and the tax collector. The package came together.

These civilizations also left problems that are still ours. Salt ruined Sumer's fields. Kings claimed to be gods. Wealth piled up in a few hands while most people farmed. The Epic of Gilgamesh, written more than four thousand years ago, is about a king who learns that even he must die and that the only lasting thing is the city and the wall he built for others. It may be the oldest answer to the question of what a life is for.

words.d: a system for dividing the year into months and days
an organized government with officials, laws, taxes and an army that rules a territory
something handed down from the past that is still with us

look.title: Gilgamesh Learns His Limit
look.text: In the epic, after his friend Enkidu dies, King Gilgamesh travels to the ends of the earth seeking a way to live forever. He is told that when the gods made humans they kept eternal life for themselves and gave death to people. He is advised to go home, eat well, dress in clean clothes, hold his child's hand and cherish his wife. That, he is told, is the lot of humankind.
look.cite: Epic of Gilgamesh, Babylonian version, about 1800 to 1200 BCE (paraphrased)
look.prompt: This advice was given to a king who built the walls of Uruk. Why might a society that had just invented cities and kings need a story like this?

check.q: Where does our 365-day calendar come from?
choices: Egyptian priests who tracked the star Sirius and the Nile flood
Hammurabi's code
The Sumerian base-sixty counting system
The Rosetta Stone
check.why: Egyptians noticed the yearly rising of Sirius near flood time and built a twelve-month calendar with five extra days.

check.q: What does the reading mean by saying Mesopotamia and Egypt invented the state?
choices: They invented the word for country
They created governments with officials, taxes, written laws and armies ruling large territories
They were the first to have kings
They built the first walls
check.why: A state is more than a ruler. It is an organized government with records, law, taxes and force, which these civilizations built first.

check.q: What lesson does Gilgamesh learn?
choices: That gods can be defeated in battle
That kings should never build walls
That humans cannot escape death and should value ordinary life
That writing is the only way to be remembered
check.why: Gilgamesh fails to find eternal life and is told to go home and cherish the life he has.

review.q: Which river's regular, gentle flood let Egyptians set a calendar by it?
choices: The Nile
The Tigris
The Euphrates
The Indus
review.why: The Nile flooded each summer with such regularity that Egyptians timed their year by it.

review.q: What is the best explanation of why irrigation led to stronger government?
choices: Kings enjoyed digging canals
Canals had to be built, repaired and shared by large organized groups
Irrigation made farming easy so people had free time
Priests owned all the water
review.why: Large-scale water systems required planning, labor and rules that only organized authority could provide.

review.q: What did the oldest cuneiform tablets record?
choices: Myths about the gods
Laws of Hammurabi
Counts of goods, animals and debts
The Epic of Gilgamesh
review.why: Writing began as bookkeeping for the temples of Uruk. Stories and laws came later.

review.q: Under Hammurabi's code, what determined the punishment for injuring someone?
choices: The age of the attacker
The city where it happened
Whether the injury was on purpose
The social rank of the victim
review.why: The same injury cost an eye, a fine or a smaller payment depending on whether the victim was noble, common or enslaved.

review.q: Which ruler united Upper and Lower Egypt around 3100 BCE?
choices: Narmer
Khufu
Ramses II
Sargon
review.why: Narmer, also remembered as Menes, joined the valley and the delta under one crown.

review.q: What does the workers' town at Giza tell us about who built the pyramids?
choices: Foreign prisoners built them under guard
Paid and fed laborers, many of them farmers in the flood season, built them
The pharaoh's family built them
Priests built them alone
review.why: Bakeries, barracks and honored graves show organized, fed workers rather than enslaved captives.

review.q: Why was Greek so important on the Rosetta Stone?
choices: Greek was the language of the pharaohs
Greek was the oldest script on the stone
Scholars could read Greek and used it to decode the Egyptian text
The stone was made in Greece
review.why: The Greek version of the decree was known, so it served as the key to the two Egyptian scripts.

review.q: Which of these is a legacy of Mesopotamia still used today?
choices: The 365-day calendar
Papyrus paper
The twenty-four hour day
Sixty minutes in an hour
review.why: Sumerian counting used base sixty, which is why hours have sixty minutes and circles have three hundred sixty degrees.
